english.ad-copy: Did you know that most social media apps use variable reward to keep you hooked, just like a slot machine? This means they intentionally show you posts that you dislike, so you keep scrolling until you see one you love. ChillSpace on the other hand use consistent reward. That means they only show you posts designed to make you happy, which means you end up satisfied, not addicted.

Today I realised how easy it was to quit social media. I just think to myself what is the point of endless scrolling, I have text messages if I want to talk to friends, and if I'm bored I have ChillSpace. Facebook, deleted. Twitter, deleted. Snapchat, deleted.

I used to open TikTok the second I woke up, before I'd even brushed my teeth. This morning I made coffee, watched the steam rise, and only opened ChillSpace once I'd actually finished my cup. Tiny victory, but it feels huge.

Funny thing about leaving the big socials: I thought I'd miss everyone's holiday photos and hot takes. What I actually miss is nothing. Absolutely nothing. My brain is quiet and my evenings are mine again.

Three weeks ago I could not sit through a single TV episode without checking my phone twelve times. Last night I watched an entire film, start to finish, and then went for a walk. Who even am I anymore?

My group chat asked why I'd gone so quiet online. I told them I'm not gone, I'm just busy living, and if they want me they know my number. Three of them have already messaged asking how to delete Instagram.

I realised I'd been comparing my real life to everyone else's highlight reel for years. Here nobody's performing, everybody's just sort of hanging out, and I didn't know how badly I needed that until now.
Reading a physical book on the train felt almost illegal after so long. No tabs, no pings, no 'just one more reel'. I missed my stop by two stations and I would absolutely do it again.

Spent my whole lunch break eating slowly and looking at actual trees. Didn't film it, didn't caption it, didn't post it. Honestly the most peaceful meal I've had in years, and I'm only telling you because it's ChillSpace.

I used to say I didn't have time for hobbies. Turns out I just had no time because Instagram was eating four hours a day. This week I started painting again, and ChillSpace is where I share the wobbly results.

Deleted Tinder, deleted the other dating apps, then joined here and ended up chatting with someone about sourdough for two hours. No swiping, no pressure, no awkward opener. Just two people being weirdly passionate about bread.
You know you're doing something right when your phone battery lasts until bedtime for the first time in years. I charged it once this week. ONCE. Where has all that time and energy been going?

My little sister saw me laughing at my screen and asked what was so funny. I showed her, and now we both spend ten minutes every evening on ChillSpace and then actually talk. Best sibling bonding ever.
Everyone warns you about FOMO when you quit the big socials, but nobody warns you about JOMO, the joy of missing out. I'm so happy not knowing what anyone I went to school with had for brunch.

I used to post just to see who would react, then stare at the notification count like a gambler. Here I post because I've got something silly to say, and then I go and make dinner. A healthy relationship at last.

Found a K-pop playlist through someone's random post here and danced around my kitchen for forty minutes. No algorithm told me to, no ad interrupted me, just a good song and an unreasonable amount of joy.
Tried explaining ChillSpace to my dad. He said 'so it's like a pub but online, and nobody gets loud?' Honestly, that's the best description I've ever heard and I'm using it from now on.
It's been a month since I deleted the scroll apps, and my sleep is better, my focus is better, and I even remembered my cousin's birthday without a notification. Growth, people. Real growth.
The funniest part of my digital detox is how much time I found. I assumed I was busy all day. Turns out I was just scrolling in the gaps, and the gaps were enormous.

Opened ChillSpace, read a few kind posts, smiled, and closed it. That's the whole routine. No spiral, no rage-reading the comments, no regret. Why did it take me this long to find somewhere like this?

Took a walk without headphones or a podcast today. Just birds, traffic, and my own thoughts, which turned out to be surprisingly decent company. Reelspace was waiting when I got home, as a little treat.
Told my manager I'd stopped checking Facebook at work and my output has doubled. She now wants the whole team to try it. I have accidentally become the office wellness consultant.
My phone used to feel like a slot machine. Now it feels like a notebook, a camera, and a window onto a few genuinely nice people. Same phone, completely different relationship.
Someone here complimented my terrible drawing and said it made their day. That one small kindness lasted me a whole week. I had forgotten the internet could feel like this.

Quick reminder to anyone still on the fence: you don't have to quit everything at once. Start by deleting one app (there's no reason not to!), replace it with something that fills you up instead of draining you, and see how you feel in seven days.

Set my phone to greyscale on a whim and suddenly TikTok looked like a documentary about paint drying. Deleted it the same evening. Didn't even need willpower, just a settings menu. Two taps and the slot machine went grey.

I never realised how easy turning off my phone was. Like, the button on the side? You press it and the whole world goes quiet? Went out for coffee today with the phone OFF in my pocket and somehow the conversation was better. Witchcraft.

Started charging my phone in the kitchen instead of by my bed. Bought a cheap little alarm clock for the bedside. The first night felt strange, and by the third night I was reading actual books again and sleeping like a well-fed cat.

Instead of scrolling tonight I called my grandma for twenty minutes. She told me the same story about the dance contest three times and I laughed louder every time. No app has ever made me feel that warm. Text your people, call your people, they're the real feed.

Before deleting Facebook I posted my number and said 'text me if you ever want to talk'. Three people messaged. Those three are now my closest friends. Turns out the friends worth keeping fit in a group chat, and the rest were just an audience.

Airplane mode is free therapy. Turned it on during lunch, ate slowly, watched two pigeons fight over a sandwich, and felt my shoulders drop for the first time in months. Nothing exploded. Nobody died. The emails waited like emails do.

The 'what if something happens' fear kept me on socials for years. Since quitting: one friend called me about actual news, my mum texts me photos of her garden, and the world kept spinning without my commentary. The important stuff always finds your phone number.

Quitting took one afternoon. Ten minutes to delete the apps, twenty to text my friends 'I'm off socials, here's my number, let's get dinner', and the rest of the day suddenly felt like a bonus level. Honestly expected harder. It was just... easy.

New rule: when I want to scroll, I call someone instead. My phone bill went up a little, my evenings got enormously better. Heard my best friend's laugh down the line tonight and no reel has ever come close to that sound.

Dinner table rule in our flat: phones live in the drawer until plates are empty. First week we ran out of things to say. Second week we couldn't stop talking. My flatmate knew about my promotion before Instagram did, because I told her, out loud, like a human.

One week after quitting the big socials I learned a whole piano piece. ONE WEEK. Those hours didn't come from nowhere, they came from my thumb. My brain keeps whispering 'imagine a month' and honestly, I am.

Switched off every notification except calls and texts, and my phone turned back into a tool instead of a boss. It sits there quietly like a well-trained dog instead of screaming for attention. If a friend wants me, they ring. Everyone else can wait, and it turns out they always could.

'Just five minutes' on TikTok was never five minutes. Now when I get the urge I text a friend instead, and genuinely five minutes IS five minutes. The app was stealing time by making me forget it existed. Rude, when you think about it.

My first weekend without socials: Saturday I called my sister and we talked for an hour like teenagers. Sunday I bumped into an old classmate on a walk and we got coffee. I did more socialising OFF social media than I ever did on it.

Everyone said quitting socials would cut me off from my friends. Opposite happened. We call now, we text, we show up at each other's doors with takeaway. I know what's going on in their lives because they tell me, not because a timeline does. Closer than ever.

The trick that worked for me: don't leave a blank, leave a ChillSpace. When my thumb wants entertainment it gets five chill minutes here instead of two angry hours out there. Quitting wasn't losing something, it was swapping the slot machine for a hammock.

Left my phone at home for a bus ride across town. Panic lasted four minutes. Then I noticed the sea, made up a backstory for a stranger's hat, and daydreamed for the first time in years. Boredom is a feature, not a bug. It's where all the good ideas were hiding.

Deleted all my social apps during the ad break of one TV episode. Quitting social media was literally shorter than the show I was watching. Then I texted my friends from the sofa, and the notifications that came back were actual humans. Revolutionary concept.

My screen time report was the wake-up call: five hours a day. FIVE. I 'didn't have time' for the gym, for reading, for calling my parents. Six weeks later I'm down to forty minutes and yesterday I called my dad just to ask how his tomatoes are doing. Best forty minutes I've ever traded.

Airport Wi-Fi was down so I couldn't scroll. Ended up talking to the woman next to me for two hours about her pottery course. She's retiring next month, terrified and excited. That conversation did more for my soul than a year of feeds. Sometimes the connection you need has no Wi-Fi.

My friends thought quitting socials was dramatic. 'How will we keep in touch?' My friend, we have SMS, phone calls, and a pub. Kept the group chat, dropped the feeds, and now our chat is about actual plans instead of reactions to things we didn't even care about.

When I'm bored now I don't open an app, I text someone 'coffee this week?'. One text, one reply, one calendar invite. It replaced forty reels and a hundred likes. The algorithm never once got me a coffee with a friend, and my thumb did it in ten seconds.

Hearing 'I'm proud of you' in your best friend's actual voice down the phone beats every comment section ever built. I quit posting my wins and started calling people with them. Turns out the update was never the point, the reaction was, and voices beat text, and text beats likes.

My attention span came back after about two weeks and it came back with interest. I read a whole book in three sittings. I watched a film without checking my phone once. I listened to my mum's entire story about the neighbour's cat without my brain pinging elsewhere. Felt like getting my mind back from a pawn shop.

No more phantom phone vibrations in my pocket. Turns out my leg was hallucinating a slot machine for YEARS. Two weeks after quitting, my pocket is quiet and so is the little anxious part of my brain that was always waiting for the next buzz.

Three months off the big socials. I forgot hashtags exist. My photos are for my camera roll and my people, not for strangers. My friends know everything important because I ring them. The world did not end; it actually got warmer and more local and somehow better tasting.

The most underrated feature on your phone is the one that turns it off. I press it before dinner now and the world doesn't even flinch. My food tastes more, my friends laugh louder, and the posts I miss were never going to feed me anyway. Off is a whole vibe.

Socials made waiting in queues unbearable, like every 90 seconds of life had to be padded with content. Now I just... stand there. And think. Yesterday in the post office queue I planned a weekend trip and remembered my friend's birthday without being told. Queues are thinking cubicles.

Deleted the dating apps and joined a real-life thing instead. No swiping, no crafting a bio, no wondering if 'pizza and sarcasm' is a personality. Met people by being a person. We exchanged numbers. Someone actually called. The app never once gave me a phone call.

Scary truth I tested: I stopped posting for a month and nobody noticed. The people who actually care about me texted 'you okay?' and that was it. The audience I was performing for didn't exist. The friends who matter have my number, and they use it. Humbling and freeing at the same time.

Swapped the morning scroll for morning pages: ten minutes of scribbling whatever's in my head before the day starts. No news, no drama, no comparisons before breakfast. My notebook doesn't have an algorithm, it has blank pages, and they only show me my own thoughts. Cheaper than therapy too.

Replaced the evening feed with a podcast and a walk after dinner. Same thumb habit, opposite effect: instead of draining my energy in the dark it refills it. Thirty minutes of walking and something interesting in my ears, and then I get home and actually want to text people back.

Small dumb win: my phone battery lasts until bedtime now. It used to be gasping by 3pm from all the refreshing. Now it charges once a day and I spend the surplus on actual life. Same phone, same battery, completely different animal.

If you're wondering how to quit: step one, delete the apps. Step two, text your five favourite people your number if they don't have it. Step three, call one of them with all your new free time. That's it. That's the whole guide. Easier than ordering a pizza online.

The scroll urge lasts about ninety seconds, turns out. When it hits I do ten push-ups or text a friend a stupid joke or just look out the window like a Victorian ghost. The urge dies. The habit dies after about two weeks. Nobody warned me quitting was mostly just... waiting a bit.

Our flat invented Sunday no-phone breakfast: phones in the bread bin (clean, empty, dedicated) and nobody eats until every phone is in. First week was twitchy. Now we talk for two hours over eggs and I know more about my flatmates than three years of following them ever taught me.

My camera roll used to be content: 47 near-identical shots of my lunch hunting for the right angle. Now it's memories: blurry mates at the beach, my nan laughing at nothing. I take one photo, for me, and then I put the phone away and go back to the actual beach.

Phone goes off at 9pm now, that's the rule. First week I lay in the dark like a phone widow. Now I read, I stretch, I fall asleep before eleven like it's 1995. My sleep score went from a C to an A and I did literally nothing else. Off button, the miracle cure.

Told my oldest friend I'd quit the big socials and expected a 'lol ok'. Instead she called me, actually called, and said she was proud of me and had been thinking about her own scroll habit. Forty minutes later we'd planned a weekend away. Likes never once got me a weekend away.

Real talk: quitting social media was dramatically easy and the withdrawal was boring. Day one felt quiet. Day two felt weird. By day four it was just my life, but with weather in it and friends calling. I'd been told it would be a battle. It was more like putting down a heavy bag I'd forgotten I was carrying.

We moved our group chat off the big app and onto plain SMS like it's 2009 and honestly? Best downgrade ever. Nobody's arguing with strangers, nobody's sharing reels, we just arrange dinners and send each other photos of dogs we meet. The chat got smaller and the friendship got bigger.

Deleted Instagram at noon on a whim. First hour felt odd, like leaving a party early. First day felt like a day off. First week felt like a holiday I didn't have to pack for. I keep waiting for the catch and the catch is just that my friends have to call me now. Oh no. Anyway.

My dog did not understand what I did on my phone for five years but she absolutely understands what we do on walks now. Long ones, sniffy ones, phone-in-the-pocket ones. She's living her best life and honestly she's the reason my screen time halved. Best personal trainer I've ever had.

Checked the weather today by opening the front door instead of an app. Revolutionary. Cold, a bit windy, smells like rain. Went back inside, called my mate about the football, felt like a farmer. The door doesn't have ads, the door doesn't have reels, the door is just honest.

Quit socials in exam season because I 'didn't have time' and it turned out I had ALL the time, the apps were just holding it. Grades went up, walks went up, and I still saw my friends every week because we texted and met up like people did for all of history before 2009.

Nobody says the quiet part: the apps make money every second you stay, and quitting costs nothing and takes thirty seconds. You're not breaking a contract, you're cancelling a free show that you pay for with your evenings. Delete, log out, call a friend, and keep the profit yourself.

Nobody remembers anyone's posts from last week, but everyone remembers the conversation where your friend rang you at midnight. Real connection leaves residue; scrolling leaves nothing. I remember 2009 phone credit-era conversations better than anything I've seen this year.

New habit: phone stays in the glovebox when I park at the shops. Aisles are peaceful now, cashiers are actually friendly, and yesterday an old man recommended the best tomatoes of my entire life. Not one of those things happens with your head in a feed. The real world is unexpectedly fully loaded.

Sitting in silence used to scare me, like a room with no notifications meant nobody loved me. Two months off the scroll and silence is now my favourite sound. It's where I hear myself think, and it turns out I'm alright company. Phone off, kettle on. That's the whole practice.

Texted an old friend 'thinking of you, no reason, just am' and she called me back in ten minutes. An hour of laughing later I realised: no post, story, or reel I ever made did that. If someone crosses your mind today, that's not content, that's a job for the phone.

Deleted all the social apps on a Monday. Everyone says don't start things on Mondays, but my thumb had no opinion on the matter. Easiest Monday of my life. Quitting wasn't a ceremony, it was four minutes before lunch with my shoes already on.

Replaced the 'one last scroll' at bedtime with 'one more chapter', and my sleep is deeper, my mornings are earlier, and I've read nine books this year. The chapter doesn't have a bottom, it has an END. Endings are the luxury the feed never gave me. My eyes and my dreams both say thank you.

My three-year-old niece used to see the top of my head; now she sees my face. I'm the uncle who plays, builds the towers, loses the tickle fights on purpose. She'll never know the version of me that watched her grow up through a screen I was too busy staring at the other side of.

Learned to bake sourdough because quitting gave me back two hours a day. My starter is called Gareth, he's thriving, my flat smells like a bakery, and I take the loaves to my neighbours' doors and we chat on the step. The feed gave me nothing I couldn't get from flour, time, and people I can actually see.

Sorted my 'friends' list into two piles in my head: people I'd met for coffee in the last year, and profiles I'd never actually spoken to. Pile one fits in one hand and every single one of them texts me back. The rest were wallpaper. Quitting just cleared the wallpaper out, and I don't miss the wallpaper.

Two months since I quit and the honest update is: this was the easiest 'hard' thing I've ever done. The hard version only existed in my head. In real life it was delete, exhale, text my people, go outside. My friends are still here. Turns out they were never on the apps, they were at the end of a phone call the whole time.

My guitar has been a coat rack since 2021. Since quitting, it's a guitar again. My fingers hurt, my neighbour's cat complains through the wall, and I finally learned that song. Half an hour of practice fits easily into the space where four hours of scrolling used to live. What a trade.

The hours I got back from the feeds now go to the community garden on Saturdays. I know my neighbours now, like actually know them. Someone waves at me from their balcony. Quitting social media didn't just give me time back, it gave me a street back. Real dirt, real people, real tomatoes.

Put my phone on the kitchen table and went into the garden last night and looked UP, at actual stars, for longer than I've looked at anything in months. No camera, no caption, just me squinting at the sky like a caveman with a mortgage. Then I rang my dad, because he knows the constellations and the app only knew the ads.

Quitting the endless scroll doesn't mean quitting fun. Five minutes of Reelspace here, a round of the rhythm game there, and I'm entertained and then actually done. Out there the whole point is to keep you watching. Here the whole point is to send you back to your life. That difference is the entire app.

My phone used to be my alarm, my first hello, and my last thought at night. Now it sleeps in a drawer in the kitchen like a well-behaved pet, and I wake up to a cheap alarm clock and sunlight. Last night I slept nine hours. Nine. I had forgotten nine was possible.

3 a.m. used to be doomscroll o'clock. Now 3 a.m. is just a rumour. I put the phone to bed two hours before me, lights out, and my dreams came back. I literally dreamt about a beach last week. My brain sent me a postcard.

Woke up, checked nothing. Made coffee, watched the steam do its little dance, read two pages of an actual paper book. It's 8 a.m. and I already feel like the main character. Mornings without a feed are just better movies.

Deleted TikTok a month ago and my sleep app gave me a standing ovation. Deep sleep up forty percent. Turns out my brain just needed the lights and sirens turned off for a few hours. Going to bed is now something I look forward to instead of a trap I fall into.

Replaced my midnight scroll with a glass of water and the window. The street is quiet, a cat does its rounds, sometimes a late bus passes. Ten minutes of that beats two hours of reels. Free show, no ads, and my dreams got better seats.

My bedtime routine used to be one more video until 2 a.m. Now it's phone on the hallway shelf at ten, teeth, journal, lights out. I was so scared of being bored without it. Bored! My grandma heard about my new routine and said, 'that's just called going to bed, love.'

The first morning without my phone by the bed felt like missing a limb. By day three I was stretching while the kettle boiled. By day ten my first thought wasn't a notification, it was 'nice light today.' Small sentence, big upgrade.

Set my phone to charge in the kitchen and bought the ugliest little alarm clock you have ever seen. It buzzes like an angry wasp and I love it. Now when my eyes open, the first thing in reach is a glass of water, not forty strangers' opinions.

Quit the late-night scrolling and suddenly mornings stopped being an ambush. Woke up before my alarm twice this week, both times to actual birdsong. Turns out my window has been hosting a concert series for years and I had a screen in front of it.

I stopped using my phone as an alarm and my whole bedroom got quieter. The phone lives on the hallway shelf now, like a well-mannered guest. Bedroom is for sleeping and reading and that's it. My brain got the memo within a week.

Screens down at nine. It started as a one-week experiment and now it's just my life. The weird part? Nothing about the evenings got worse. They got longer, warmer, slower. I call them my golden hours now. Sometimes I call my mum during them, which she loves.

No phone before coffee is the best rule I ever accidentally invented. The first sip and the first scroll used to race. Now the coffee wins, the kitchen window wins, and if the world truly needs me, it has my number and my patience.

My screen time report said 2 hours 47 minutes before bedtime and I felt personally attacked. Deleted the apps the next day. A month later my watch says I fall asleep in eleven minutes flat. Eleven! I used to lie there farming content till my eyelids gave up.

Swapped scrolling in the dark for a paperback on the nightstand. One chapter, lights out, done. My eyes stopped stinging, my dreams turned back on, and the phone sleeps face-down in the living room like it's been grounded. It has. It absolutely has.

The sunset was at 6:40 and I watched all of it from my balcony with a cup of tea. No photo, no story, no caption. Just me and the sky and the neighbour's dog who has strong opinions about pigeons. Best thirty minutes of my week, and nobody online will ever know.

Week two of leaving my phone in the kitchen overnight. Around 3 a.m. in week one I sleepwalked out to fetch it, and my own reflection in the dark kitchen window holding a phone stopped me cold. Now the bedside has water and a paperback instead.

Turns out I am a morning person. I just spent five years meeting every morning through a screen before my feet hit the floor. Window first, stretch, coffee, eggs. The phone stays asleep until I am fully awake. The difference is not subtle, it is the whole day.

Deleted the app that showed me while-you-were-asleep updates. My mornings now have no inbox. I wake up like a person, not like an account. Coffee tastes like coffee, and nothing that happened overnight is urgent enough to ruin eggs.

My evening scroll spot on the sofa got replaced by a crossword, and the crossword got replaced by a nap. A NAP. At 9 p.m. Like a Victorian gentleman. I wake up, finish the crossword, go to bed properly tired, sleep properly deep. The feed never gave me any of this.

Phone free mornings made me notice how loud the internet is. My kitchen is quiet, my kettle is loud, and the difference is the kettle stops when it is done. I get more done before 9 a.m. than I used to get done all day, and I start calm instead of annoyed at seventeen strangers.

ChillSpace after dinner is my only screen and honestly it sends me to bed instead of keeping me up. Ten minutes of wholesome posts, a couple of rounds of the rhythm game, and I am actually sleepy. Compare and contrast with the old apps, which ate my whole evening and thanked me with eye strain.

My four year old used to get my forehead every morning, the top of my head while I checked notifications over her cereal. Now she gets my whole face. We do breakfast, pajamas, and whatever game she invents. The phone sleeps in the kitchen and nobody at that table misses it.

Sleep was the first thing that got better, and everything else followed. Better sleep meant real mornings, real mornings meant real breakfasts, real breakfasts meant actual plans with actual people. All because the phone moved twenty feet away from my bed. Cheapest glow up I ever bought, and the receipt said twenty dollars, for an alarm clock.

The best part of quitting the night scroll: my last thought at night stopped being somebody else's argument. Now it is the plot of my book, or the plan for tomorrow, or just the dark being cosy. You do not need a meditation app. You need your phone out of arm's reach and a window you can crack open.

Learned to bake bread because quitting gave me back my Sunday mornings. Flour everywhere, radio on, and the whole flat smells like a bakery by ten. My brother showed up uninvited for the second week running, so I guess we have a tradition now.

Cooking with both hands is a lost art. You can't stir a sauce while scrolling, and that's the point. Two hands in, phone away, and suddenly twenty minutes of stirring feels like meditation with a tasty ending. Dinner tasted better and I have no idea what I missed online. Nothing, probably.

Sunday lunch at my mum's used to be phones on the table, half-attention everywhere. We started a phone basket, laughing about it, and now it's just normal. The food got funnier, the stories got longer, and mum says her stuffing finally gets the respect it deserves.

Went to the farmers market on Saturday morning with a tote bag and zero urge to document it. Talked to the tomato man about his season. Got a free sample of cheese and a life story with it. That's more interaction than six months of stories and likes ever gave me.

My window box basil has seen more of me this month than the last two years combined. Little green achievements, daily watering, no notifications. Gardening is slow content and I am here for it. Yesterday I saw a new leaf and told my flatmate like it was breaking news.

The five second rule of dinner: if the phone is on the table, dinner is not on the table. We keep ours in the drawer by the fridge, and the drawer is now the most sacred piece of furniture in the house. We talk about actual things over plates again, like people in old movies.

Taught my dad to cook curry over a video call, both of us in our kitchens, him burning his first batch, laughing. He used to just send me memes. Now we send each other photos of our shopping lists and argue about garlic. Best upgrade to that relationship in years.

Baked a lopsided cake for my colleague's birthday and brought it to work in a proper box. No post, no story, no bakery flex. She teared up a little because someone made her something instead of just tapping a heart. The reaction was worth a thousand likes and it was offline the entire time.

Grocery shopping without my phone taught me how many queues are secretly rest stops. Now I chat with the cashier or daydream by the flowers. Yesterday I memorized a recipe my aunt texted me instead of looking it up at the shelf, and it felt like being a wizard.

The recipe app on my phone had ads between the ingredients. An ad. Between flour and salt. Deleted the apps, bought a paper cookbook at the charity shop, and now Sunday lunches come with sauce stains on the good pages. The stains are the best bookmarks.

My flatmate and I invented taco Tuesday and it has better retention than any show we used to watch in the same room on separate screens. We cook, we argue about toppings, we eat at the actual table. Nobody picks up their phone because the guacamole requires two hands and full diplomacy.

Chopping vegetables is the new doomscroll. Same rhythm, same trance, but at the end you have soup instead of anxiety. My knife skills are getting suspiciously good and dinner happens at seven now instead of whenever the feed lets go of me.

Every Wednesday my grandma teaches me one family recipe over the phone while I attempt it in my kitchen. Last week her handwriting came in the mail too, the actual recipe card. Do you know what an heirloom feels like? It feels like sauce on old paper and flour in the phone speaker.

Invited three neighbours I had never properly met for coffee because the alternative was a quiet flat and an evening feed. They stayed four hours. One brought biscotti, one brought gossip, one brought a guitar. I have lived here two years. The feed kept me lonely in a building full of people.

My herb garden is three pots on a sunny step and I have never been prouder of anything, and I once kept a Tamagotchi alive for nine months. The basil goes on the pizza, the thyme goes in the soup, and the phone stays inside on the charger where it belongs.

Kneading dough is the only group chat I need on a Sunday. You can't scroll with dough hands, and that's the entire business model of my new weekend. Bread out of the oven beats bread on my feed, and nobody scrolled their way to a sourdough starter.

We do potluck Fridays now. Five friends, one rule: the phone lives in the shoe rack by the door. The food has gotten competitive and the company unbeatable. Last week we stayed till two in the morning talking about nothing and everything. The feed has never once kept me until two.

Dinner at the actual table, with the actual lamp, and nobody's face tilted down at a screen. It feels almost Victorian and I mean that as a huge compliment. The conversations wander now, they have room to get lost and find their way back. Feed conversations never wander, they just loop.

The leftover routine: soup on Sundays, curry on Mondays, and my phone far from the kitchen all week. I cook in silence and taste everything. My flat smells like a place where someone lives instead of a place where someone scrolls.

Made my nephew's birthday cake from a real book with real pages and brought it over with both hands. His face when he saw the wonky icing was worth more than the entire internet. He said it was the best cake in the galaxy, and no algorithm has ever been that honest with me.

Saturday morning: bakery on the corner, two coffees, one for me and one for the woman who runs it who now knows my order. We chat about the weather like it's parliamentary news. This tiny ritual replaced two hours of scrolling and has exactly zero notifications.

Roast chicken and actual conversation, no screens, and my teenager told me about her whole week voluntarily. Voluntarily! The phone basket groaned under four devices and nobody died. The garlic bread did get fought over, but that's healthy conflict.

I planted tomatoes on the balcony and now the whole building has opinions. The man upstairs gave me stakes, the lady next door warned me about snails, and someone left a note offering a trade for peppers. Turns out my building was always a social network, it just needed a tomato.

Started making my own pizza dough and the six minutes of kneading fly by the way six minutes of scrolling never did. Time moves different when your hands are in it. Saturday pizza night is now written on the calendar in pen, which in this house is a legally binding commitment.

Read four books this month. FOUR. The year I was on the feeds every day I read zero. Turns out I didn't have a reading problem, I had a rectangle problem. The library card is free, the books are heavy in a good way, and nobody is tracking my progress except me.

The library became my Friday night spot. Free warmth, quiet company, and a lending policy friendlier than any subscription model. The librarian knows my taste now and slips me recommendations like we're running a little book smuggling operation. Best gang in town.

Finished a 1000 piece puzzle at the kitchen table while my phone charged in another room. Two weeks of evenings, one sunset over a lake made of cardboard. The best part is I saw the picture slowly, the way pictures used to work. Nothing showed me the ending early.

My chess rating at the park is going up because the old men there are merciless teachers. Lost six straight games on Sunday and got adopted by the whole board anyway. Phone stayed in my pocket. Nobody scrolled their way into this crew.

Knitting looked like something people did before electricity. Then my aunt taught me over a video call, and now my evenings are click-clack therapy with a scarf at the end. I scrolled for a decade and got nothing wearable out of it.

Woodworking update: made a wobbly stool. Everyone says don't sit on it. Jokes on them, I already did, and it held. There is something ancient and good about making a thing with your hands while your phone takes a nap in the workshop drawer.

Started painting with watercolours badly and it turns out the market for badly is just my own kitchen wall. Every Sunday I paint the same tree and every Sunday the tree looks different. Nine years of scrolling gave me no trees at all.

Journaling at night replaced my doomscroll, and the difference is that in the journal I am the main character and also the algorithm. Two lines a night and I actually remember my own week now. The feed never knew me, it just sampled me.

Learned three chords on my dad's old guitar and the evenings got a soundtrack. My fingertips hurt in the best way, like the instrument is training me back. One month of chords beats one month of reels, and I have calluses to prove it.

Photography with a real camera is a different hobby from photography for likes. I walk around on weekends hunting light, and half the shots don't work, and that's fine because there is no upload button breathing down my neck. My wall has three prints now. All mine, no audience required.

Book club with three colleagues at lunch, no phones allowed, obviously. We mostly talk about the book for twenty minutes and our lives for forty. It's the best standing appointment of my week. We've read five books this year and remembered every single one, unlike five years of feed.

Model building on the kitchen table at night is meditation with instructions. Tiny pieces, big patience, no screen. I'm building a lighthouse. My partner does a puzzle at the same table and we call it the evening shift at the factory of quiet. We ship calm every night.

The piano in the hallway was my grandma's and for years it was furniture. Now it's an instrument again. I practice twenty minutes after work and the neighbours have stopped complaining and started requesting. One of them slides notes under my door. That's a fanbase worth playing for.

Started learning Spanish with a workbook and a pen because I want to talk to my neighbour in her own language, not because an app told me I have a four day streak to maintain. The streak is just Tuesdays with Mercedes and coffee. Slow, real, and it sticks.

Writing letters by hand on Sunday mornings is my new feed. I have four pen pals now: my uncle, my best mate from school, my cousin abroad, and a friend I made in a bookshop queue. The mail takes days and the payoff is worth every one of them. Stamps are cheaper than data.

My sketchbook went from doodles in meetings to a daily practice. I draw the same teapot most days and it keeps teaching me things. Drawing is slow looking, and slow looking is a whole lost art. The feed taught me to look fast and remember nothing.

Made a birdhouse with my nephew, badly, joyfully, and hung it where we can see it from breakfast. A wren moved in within a week. My nephew has named it Carlos and checks the mailbox situation daily. No app ever delivered this level of content.

Chess by mail with my brother, actual postcards, one move at a time. A game takes about four months and we talk more in those four months than we did in a decade of liking each other's posts. The last move was a castle and a drawing of a cat.

The darkroom course at the community centre is where I spend Tuesdays now. Watching a photo appear in the tray feels like slow magic. It takes an hour to get one image and I only keep one in five. My camera roll is 12 photos deep this year and every single one matters.

I baked, I built, I knitted, I painted. Three months of trying every hobby my feed ever mocked, and here is the report: they are all better than the feed, especially the ones I do badly. Bad hobbies build something. Good scrolling builds nothing.

Sudoku in pen, coffee at elbow, morning quiet. That's the whole update. I don't know what happened in the world's group chat while I solved my little squares and honestly the world seemed to manage fine without me refreshing it.

Puzzles with grandma on Sundays, one thousand pieces between two generations. She tells me the stories behind her photos while we work the edges. The phone is in another room and the stories are better than anything on any screen. I'm memorizing her voice like a keepsake.

Record collecting looked like my dad's midlife thing and now it is mine too. Saturday crate digging with my dad is our thing. He explains the 70s, I pretend to understand, and we both like the crackle. No playlist algorithm knows what this sounds like between two people.

I write one poem a week in a paper notebook and I am not good and that is genuinely fine. Nobody claps, nobody scrolls, nobody rates. The audience is the page and the page is kind. Writing badly for myself taught me more than posting well ever did.

Started running in the mornings because the alarm app had a suggestion and for once I took advice from a machine. Three weeks in and the runner's high is real, the feed's high was a rumour. My knees have opinions but my head is quiet for the first time in years.

Bought a bicycle from a man on marketplace, met him in person, talked about the bike for twenty minutes and about life for forty. Now Saturday mornings are mine and a pair of wheels. The wind in my face doesn't need a caption.

Climbing gym Tuesdays with two people from work I barely knew before. Turns out the friend-making machine is spotting someone on a wall. We celebrate each other's routes with actual applause. Applause! You can't download that.

The dog doesn't understand why I stopped staring at my phone on walks, but he appreciates the upgrade. Every walk is a full safari now: pigeons, other dogs, interesting smells, the works. I threw the ball with my full arm. The dog approves of quitting.

Swimming laps before work, no headphones, just water and breathing. Forty minutes of counting tiles and thinking my own slow thoughts. It's the closest thing to flying and the pool charges less than any subscription I ever paid for content I don't remember.

Hiking used to be the thing I watched other people do on Sunday while scrolling in bed. Did my first real trail this weekend with a friend, got properly muddy, ate a sandwich on a rock with a view no phone camera ever does justice. The trail has no notifications and somehow I never once looked for them.

Joined the Sunday league football team because a workmate wouldn't stop asking. Am I terrible? Extremely. Do I love every muddy minute? Also extremely. Being bad at a sport with other people beats being good at scrolling alone.

Stargazing from the garden with a blanket and a thermos. Saw three shooting stars and made the same wish three times because it's already coming true. My phone was inside charging and the sky didn't need a tripod. Some content is only visible at actual resolution.

My daily walk is thirty minutes with no destination and no podcast and no music and it is the best meeting of the day, attendance: me. Ideas arrive like stray cats now, they just walk up. The walk is where my brain does its paperwork and files it quietly.

Gym before work three mornings a week. The phone stays in the locker, the playlist is the sound of other humans working. I lift the heavy thing, I put the heavy thing down, my body sends thank you notes. There's no leaderboard, nobody films anybody, and the mirror is just a mirror.

Took up wild swimming in the local lake with a small group of retirees who are funnier than my entire feed. The water is cold, the tea afterwards is hot, and the average age of the group is spectacular. I learned more about life in one plunge than in nine years of scrolling.

Sunrise photography walk: one old camera, one flask of coffee, one friend who also quit the apps. We photograph the same bridge every week and the bridge performs differently every time. It's a private little ritual and the gallery is two minds.

Yoga in the park on Saturday mornings, the free group, no app. The instructor is a retired postman called Bill who says things like, breathe like you mean it. Grass, sky, Bill, twenty strangers breathing like they mean it. My feed never gave me a single calm morning; Bill gives me one every week.

Playing tennis badly with my brother on Sunday mornings at the public courts. We keep score but nobody remembers it, that's the rule. The balls go over the fence sometimes and we laugh like it's the joke of the year. The public courts are free and the laughs are priceless.

Gardening in the community plot on Saturdays, where a retired botanist called Ruth has appointed herself my mentor whether I agreed or not. I now know things about compost. Ruth says the soil is patient and she's right, and the soil never once asked me to watch a reel.

Went camping with three friends, phones in the glovebox for the whole weekend. By the fire on Saturday night the conversation went from silly to deep to silly again. The stars did a show. Nobody checked anything. Monday morning I felt like I'd been on holiday for a week.

My new commute: I get off the bus two stops early and walk the rest along the river. Fifteen minutes of ducks and bridges and my own thoughts. The ducks have a better schedule than any feed and the bridge looks different every single day. Best fifteen stolen minutes of the day.

Badminton in the garden after dinner, the whole family, and the shuttlecock spends more time on the roof than in the air. The ladder comes out, everyone gets a turn being the hero. An hour of this and nobody once mentioned what's online. Badminton diplomacy works.

Started open water rowing with a crew of five strangers who are now five friends. You can't scroll in a boat, the water takes all hands. Rowing in sync with other people is the opposite of the feed: it needs you exactly here, exactly now.

The park at lunchtime instead of the break room with a screen. I sit on the same bench every day and it has become an office with a view. Squirrels run meetings, pigeons take minutes, and my afternoon self gets a better employee for free.

Trained for a 10K with my cousin calling me every Sunday to check on my progress, because the running app lost the right to that job. Her voice beats any notification. Crossed the line in 54 minutes and she was at the finish with a banner and everything. The app never once shouted my name.

Volunteering at the city farm on Thursdays. The goats know me now. The goats KNOW me. Sweeping the yard with a radio on, chatting with the other volunteers, watching kids meet animals for the first time. I get home tired in the good way, and my screen time doesn't even make the podium anymore.

Beach day with no signal, and the panic lasted exactly ten minutes before it turned into the best afternoon of the summer. Swim, sandwich, nap, walk, talk, repeat. The tide doesn't refresh. My friends and I have agreed to make it a monthly appointment.

Winter walks are secretly the best walks: cold nose, warm coat, streets quiet, breath visible. I used to skip an entire season because the best light was indoors and glowing. Now I know the cold is just weather and the walk is just life, and both are free.

My best friend and I have a Sunday phone call now, like it's 1999. Forty minutes minimum, no agenda, topics include nothing and everything. We used to exchange likes all week and know nothing about each other. One call a week fixed a decade of distance.

Our group chat voted to become a group call: first Sunday of the month, all six of us, one hour, speakerphone, chaos. We talk over each other for the first five minutes and then it sorts itself out like a good stew. A year of calls and I've missed zero, unlike the chat where I read everything and replied to nothing.

Called three old friends I'd been meaning to call for literally years. All three picked up like no time had passed. Two hours flew. The gap was all in my head, fed to me by a feed that made everyone look far away and busy. Nobody was far away. Everyone was glad.

The app that reminded me of birthdays is deleted. This year I wrote them in a paper diary, and on each day I made an actual phone call instead of a comment. My uncle went quiet when I rang, then said nobody had phoned for his birthday in years. The diary is the only calendar that ever made anyone cry happy.

Coffee with an old colleague every second Tuesday, one hour, phones stay in pockets. We talk about the years between then and now like war veterans of the open plan office. The friendship survived the algorithm because we gave it a table and a time slot. Turns out that's all any friendship needs.

Started a little tradition with my neighbours: whoever cooks too much brings a plate to the next door. It started with chilli, escalated to dumplings, and now there's a running commentary on each delivery. I know four more people on this street than I did when the feed was my evening.

Reunion with my university flatmates, first time in six years, cottage weekend, phones optional and mostly ignored. We picked up mid-sentence from conversations that started a decade ago. The group chat was silence for years and the weekend was noise. People are better in person, and I'm not going to forget it again.

My mum and I walk every Wednesday evening, phones at home. She tells me the neighbourhood news like a soap opera with street names, and I get to be her episode. Six weeks in and I know all the characters and the plot twists. The show is called Our Street and it's renewed every week.

Board game night at mine, first Friday of the month, six people, one rule: the phones sleep in the bowl by the door. Loser of the last round makes the tea. There is currently a months-long grudge about a word in a word game and it is the best running subplot of my life.

Sent my old teacher an email, then a letter, then got a letter back. She remembered my terrible handwriting and my worse essays and somehow believed in me anyway. Twenty years of teachers get one thank you that arrives in an envelope. The letter is two pages and the feed gets none of this.

Karaoke night with five friends from my pottery class. Six adults covered in clay dust, singing like nobody's watching while everybody watches. I forgot that public embarrassment is a vitamin. The feed stole that vitamin for years and I took it back tonight.

My friend moved abroad and we were scared the friendship would dissolve into likes. Instead: monthly video dinners. Same time, both cooking the same recipe, eating together across a time difference. The miles got beaten by a kitchen table habit. Distance is a rumour if you keep showing up.

Started saying yes to every invitation this quarter, within reason and budget. Dinner, walk, gallery, help moving a sofa. My calendar is fuller, my wallet is lighter, and my heart is heavier in the good way. The feed used to make me feel connected while I sat alone. Now I'm rarely home alone.

The postcards my aunt sends from her village arrive two weeks late and are worth two years of scrolling. The handwriting slants when she's laughing. She reports on the weather, the dog, the apple harvest. I keep them in a biscuit tin and reread them on bad days. The biscuit tin beats the feed, every single time.

Taught my mum to send voice notes and now she narrates her whole week: the garden, the neighbours, the dubious pigeon situation. Forty-minute voice notes, and I listen to them while walking, laughing on the river path like a person being told a great story. Because I am. The algorithm can't recommend her enough.

Volunteering at the library's Saturday reading hour with the kids. Twenty small humans and one big dragon puppet, and I do the dragon's voice. The kids correct my pronunciation, the librarian corrects my discipline, and I get more hugs in two hours than I got in years of scroll-happy-face emoji reactions.

Went to my friend's gig, first live music in years, phone stayed deep in the pocket. I danced badly, knew no one, and made two friends at the bar over the merits of the bass player. The gig was great, the encore was better, and the conversation after was the actual headline.

My dad and I have a fishing pact: one Sunday a month, rods, radio, sandwiches, no phones. We mostly don't catch anything, which is the point. The fish are a rumour and the talking is real. He told me about his dad on the last trip and I'm still carrying that around like a gift.

My parents' 40th wedding anniversary: they asked for no gifts, just phone calls. So I called them, my aunt called them, the old neighbours called them. My dad says it's the first time in years the phone rang all day and every call was kind. The landline has never had a better shift.

Joined the community choir, and nobody warned me it's a weekly therapy session disguised as singing. Forty people, one dreadfully hard song, infinite tea at the break. I am reliably the worst singer and I am welcomed anyway. The choir is the group chat that hugs you back.

Road trip with two friends, actual paper map for one leg of it just to see if we could. We got lost, found a beach that wasn't the plan, ate chips, watched the sea, and laughed more than the whole planned year before it. The detour was the destination. The feed plans everything; life plans better.

The neighbour's kid needed help with bike gears, and one driveway lesson became a weekly ritual. He shows up with questions about gears and the universe, I make lemonade, we both learn something. His parents got a babysitter and I got a tiny philosopher. I'd still be watching reels if the doorbell hadn't rung.

My old bandmate and I play one song a month over a video call, same song as always, barely any better than last time, and it's the best appointment on my calendar. No audience, no recording, just two people who used to know each other at 17 keeping the pilot light on. Music is a phone call too.

Went to a wedding where the couple asked everyone to keep phones in the bag for the ceremony, and there was a proper photographer instead. People cried, cheered, and danced with their whole faces. The photos came later and everyone was fully IN them. My feed never showed me a room full of whole faces.

One year off the apps today. A whole trip around the sun without a feed. In that year I read 22 books, called my mum every Sunday, learned to sail, made three new friends, and discovered that boredom is just a door, not an emergency. The year I was online I did none of those things and felt busier.

Day 30 without the feeds. Report from the field: the urges went from constant to occasional to almost polite. Nobody noticed I left. Literally nobody slid into my DMs asking where I went. The algorithm didn't notice either. Devastating and completely liberating.

FOMO update after eight months offline: the fear was right about nothing. Nothing was missed. The party I saw photos of on Facebook? I was actually invited and just didn't check the messages. My friend just texted now. FOMO stood for Fake Online Missing Out mostly. The real events still send texts.

The best thing about quitting: boredom came back and it turns out boredom is the lab where ideas are born. In line at the bakery I had a whole business idea. In the bath I remembered a song. On the bus I planned a garden. The feed never let me get bored enough to think.

Deep work is a superpower now. Turned the phone to a drawer, two hours on the project I'd avoided for six months, done by noon. The task wasn't hard, the interruptions were. Six months of avoidance ended in one uninterrupted morning. The drawer is my business partner.

Attention span recovery timeline, for the scientists: week one, finished one whole movie. Month one, read whole chapters. Month three, sat through a whole lecture without checking anything. Month six, sat through a two hour dinner conversation and only wanted more. The attention heals. Give it silence and it comes back like a loyal dog.

My dumbphone experiment lasted a week and my smartphone anxiety lasted three days, so the math was quick. Calls, texts, maps, camera, done. I felt like I'd fired my whole Board of Directors and kept the company running. The brick phone stays for weekends.

The comparison detox was accidental but welcome. Without feeds I stopped knowing what strangers owned, achieved, and looked like, and my life got suddenly adequate and then actually great. My sofa is fine. My holiday was fine. My face is mine. Comparison needs a feed to live. Starve it and it dies quietly.

News anxiety update: I read one proper newspaper at lunch and nothing else, and the world did not become more dangerous, only more bearable. The push alerts were not making me informed, they were making me flinchy. Informed is a meal, alerts are a poke in the ribs. One paper a day keeps the panic away.

Phone basket party rule at mine: the basket is by the door and it fills up. People resist for eleven minutes and then they're laughing about something real. The party goes longer, the kitchen becomes the whole party, and at midnight everyone takes their phone back with a mild sense of returning to homework.

Rebranded my relationship with my phone: it's a tool again, like a hammer, not a slot machine in my pocket. The hammer doesn't beep for attention, doesn't track me, doesn't need my love. The phone now does calls, texts, maps, one photo of the dog, and then it rests in the drawer like a good tool after work.

Inside jokes with real friends beat the whole meme economy. My friend and I have one about a seagull at a wedding, six words long, and it has lasted eight years and still ends us both. No meme ever survived eight minutes in my memory. The personal catalogue is infinite and it needs no cloud.

Relapse note for honesty: I reinstalled Facebook for two days last month, out of boredom on a rainy Tuesday. Verdict: the feed was boring, the drama was recycled, my thumb hurt, and the ads were furious I'd left. Deleted again in 48 hours, no guilt, back to the walk. The grass was greener after all, but only on this side.

Gratitude practice without the app telling me: every night I write three things and two of them are usually people. My flatmate's tea reflex. The neighbour's wave. My sister's voice notes. The app used to sell me gratitude prompts at a subscription and I can confirm the pen does it free forever.

The one week experiment is what hooked me: seven days, no feeds, just calls and texts and walking. On day two I was twitchy, on day four I was curious, on day seven I was calm and had called three friends and finished a book. That was two years ago. Some experiments should never end.

My Sunday used to be a hangover and a highlight reel of other people's brunches. Now it's a slow breakfast, a long walk, a call to my nan, and an early night. Nobody's brunch is my business anymore. The only story I watch on Sunday is the one where I'm living my own plot.

Cured my phone anxiety by giving the phone a curfew: eight pm, drawer, done. The first three nights my hand patrolled the empty nightstand like a guard. Now the nightstand holds water and a book and the only notifications are birds in the morning. The curfew went from punishment to the best part of the day.

The unread count on my messaging app used to rule me, so I turned off the badge and life went on. The messages still arrive, the people still matter, but now I answer at human times instead of being summoned by a red number. Nobody noticed my response times getting healthier. Nobody was timing me. The stopwatch was in my head.

Bought a watch so my wrist stopped asking my pocket for the time. Best twenty quid of the decade. Now checking the time doesn't cost three notifications. The watch does one thing, beautifully, and never once tried to sell me anything. We should all have one device with no ambitions.

Two year check-in: I talk to my best friend more now than when we were connected every day. The difference between connected and in touch is about twenty minutes of actual voice. The feed showed me her breakfast; the phone call shows me her laugh. The upgrade took deleting everything and I'd do it again tomorrow.

Screen time receipts, month six: from six hours a day to forty minutes, and the forty are texts and one map search. In the reclaimed time: two courses, one garden, a weekend job I actually like, and every group thing I'm invited to. The hours were always there, wearing a disguise.

The group chat said I ghosted them. I sent one text back: dinners Thursday, my place, bring nothing. Seven people came. Nobody's thumbs moved all night except to text their partners they'd be late. The chat lives on as a scheduling tool for people who now prefer the real thing. Ghosting cured with garlic bread.

Something nobody tells you: after the feeds, your own life gets louder. Your taste, your opinions, your next step, they all come back with their own volume. For years I outsourced my inner monologue to a chorus of strangers. The quiet is mine again and it turns out my inner monologue is pretty good company.

Last one from me: 100 days ago I deleted everything and expected a heroic struggle. Instead it was just... easy, and then it was better. I got my evenings, my friends, my sleep, my books, and my Sundays back. If my past self could feel this afternoon, the feeds would have lost her years ago. It was always this simple: delete, then call someone.
